title: Compact fusion drive for spacecraft
bottleneck: A fusion rocket, such as the Direct Fusion Drive concept burning deuterium and helium-3, could deliver both high thrust and high efficiency, enabling months-long Mars trips and credible interstellar precursor missions. But no fusion reactor produces net energy on Earth, let alone one compact, lightweight, vacuum-rated, and reliable enough to fly. The gap includes confining plasma in a space-rated device, rejecting enormous waste heat through radiators, and surviving neutron damage over long burns.
why_it_blocks: Chemical and even fission propulsion impose hard delta-v limits; fusion is the first technology that could make the outer solar system routinely accessible and cut interplanetary travel to practical timescales.
current_state: Government fusion roadmaps put demonstration reactors decades away, and none address spacecraft integration. Concepts remain paper studies and small lab experiments; no space-rated fusion prototype exists.
